title: FIPS & BYO-HSM Key Ops Review — Meridian Aviation Security Sync

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Lina Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CISO), Carlos Mendez (Head of Infra), Ethan Ross (Security Eng)

Summary (auto): FIPS/BYO-HSM deep dive, data residency clarifications, rotation cadence and audit log retention discussed. Action items and staging test agreed.

[00:00] Jordan Park: hey everybody, thanks for joining — appreciate you making time, especially with the timezone. quick intro, i'm jordan from redwood, ae on the account, and lina will be our se, she'll take the tech deep dive.

[00:18] Priya Kapoor: thanks, jordan. i'll be quick — high level priorities: we need FIPS-validated HSMs, regional key residency in EU and APAC for certain markets, and audit trails that satisfy our internal auditors and external auditors. also minimal service interruption during rotation.

[00:34] Jordan Park: perfect, that's basically what we wanted to cover. lina, do you want to open with the architecture sketch for BYOK + HSM?

[00:40] Lina Chen: yeah absolutely. i'll share my screen — can everyone see the diagram? it's a simple flow: customer keys are provisioned in their HSM, we support both PKCS#11 and KMIP connectors, the keys can stay in the customer's HSM, we use an HSM client to perform wrap/unwrap operations, and redwood's control plane stores only key references and metadata — never raw key material.

[01:05] Carlos Mendez: sorry to interrupt, when you say control plane stores only references, is that metadata encrypted? like, what kms encrypts the metadata?

[01:12] Lina Chen: good question. the metadata is encrypted at rest with a service-managed envelope key. if you choose BYOK, the envelope key can be a customer-managed key in your HSM, so the metadata envelope is wrapped by your HSM key. i should note, the stored artefacts include key IDs, rotation timestamps, audit hashes, but not private key bytes.

[01:38] Ethan Ross: and for in-transit we need mTLS to our connector, is that supported? our ops team requires mutual TLS between our on-prem HSM proxy and vendor endpoints.

[01:46] Lina Chen: yes, we support mTLS. the connector establishes a mutual TLS tunnel, client certs are rotated and can be pinned in the seeding process. there's also a VPN option if you need private connectivity — some customers use VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink.

[02:10] Priya Kapoor: our compliance lead flagged FIPS 140-3 specifically — do you have a FIPS attestation for the connector and for the HSMs you integrate with?

[02:18] Jordan Park: i'll take that — we maintain a compatibility matrix. we don't FIPS-validate the connector itself as a module under the customer's program, but we integrate with FIPS-validated HSMs (e.g., Thales, SafeNet, Luna, etc.). we can provide the FIPS-validated part numbers and certs. lina, correct me if i'm muddying.

[02:37] Lina Chen: that's right. the connector is a customer-side component; customers include it in their own attestation if they need. redwood can provide a guidance document and the list of HSM models we've tested. customers doing formal FIPS enclave attestation usually include the HSM and their deployment architecture in scope.

[03:00] Carlos Mendez: ok that helps. about rotation — we have a hard requirement: keys for production must rotate without any downtime and we must be able to demonstrate rotation logs for audit. how does your rotation flow look?

[03:10] Lina Chen: we support seamless key rotation using a staged rotation — create new key in HSM, update key reference and rotate wrap key, then re-wrap cached prefixes if needed. for active sessions we rely on KV cache TTL; we can do a canary rollout so a percentage of requests use new key first. rotation events are recorded in write-once audit logs.

[03:33] Ethan Ross: "write-once" meaning append-only immutable store? where do those logs live and who can access them?

[03:39] Lina Chen: logs are pushed to your configured retention store — typical patterns are S3 (with object lock for immutability) or a SIEM like Splunk/Elastic via signed streams. access is controlled by RBAC; by default only the account admins and auditors can retrieve them. we also send signed digests to an external key for tamper-evidence.

[03:58] Priya Kapoor: we require 7 years of retention for certain flight-safety records — is that feasible? object lock plus long-term S3 is fine, but we need chain-of-custody and cryptographic proofs.

[04:08] Lina Chen: yes, customers have used S3 object lock + Glacier deep archive. for chain-of-custody we maintain a signed audit chain where each log block is hashed and signed; you can independently verify the hashes. we'll include the verification scripts in the runbook.

[04:32] Jordan Park: quick side note: we have a SOC2 package and ISO27001 artifacts we can share. i'll attach those to the ticket after the call — they include architecture diagrams and control mappings relevant to key mgmt.

[04:44] Priya Kapoor: please do. we also need to confirm SSO and RBAC integration — our auditors will check admin actions on key operations. can we map operations to SAML roles?

[04:52] Lina Chen: yes, we support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning and role-based policies. admin operations (create/rotate/escrow/restore) are gated by RBAC and MFA. we also emit audit events for each action with a user and session id.

[05:10] Carlos Mendez: about escrow — we have a procurement requirement for key escrow under certain conditions. what's your recommended escrow model? can we escrow encrypted key backups to a third-party vault?

[05:19] Lina Chen: recommended pattern: primary key lives in your HSM, periodic encrypted backups are stored in your S3 or a third-party escrow vault. those backups are themselves wrapped with a secondary key in your HSM or an escrow HSM. access to escrowed backups requires a multi-party approval workflow which we can gate via integration with your ticketing and KMS approval flows.

[05:43] Ethan Ross: multi-party approval is a must. can that be enforced via HSM policies (i.e., require n-of-m in the HSM) or is it a process outside the HSM?

[05:51] Lina Chen: depends on the HSM. many HSMs support quorum policies; for others we implement approval gates in the orchestration layer and require dual sign-off. for true cryptographic enforcement, you'd use HSM-native quorum. we can document both approaches for your auditors.

[06:13] Priya Kapoor: what about cross-region keys — for e.g., keys must not leave EU region for EU customers. can you ensure the key material never leaves the customer HSM in that region?

[06:24] Jordan Park: yes — in the BYOK model the key is in your HSM and never exported. redwood will route requests to the HSM proxy in the same region. if you need geo-fencing we can restrict routing policy and prevent fallbacks that would send tokens to other regions.

[06:44] Carlos Mendez: any latency implications if every sign/unwrap has to hit our on-prem HSM vs a cloud HSM?

[06:51] Lina Chen: there is latency — signing per-call to an on-prem HSM will add RTT. we typically recommend a hybrid approach: use the HSM for master key material and wrap a high-throughput, short-lived data key that lives in a secure cache in the serving layer. that gives you cryptographic control without per-token HSM hits. the cache TTL can be tuned to your risk profile.

[07:19] Ethan Ross: cache TTLs sound sensible — from a crypto audit perspective we need to record when data keys are derived and which HSM key wrapped them. are those derivation events in the audit log?

[07:28] Lina Chen: yes, each derive/wrap event is logged with key id, origin HSM id, requesting principal, and a timestamp. we also emit the key thumbprint so auditors can correlate.

[07:45] Priya Kapoor: curious about the HSM connector lifecycle — what's the upgrade story? if the connector has a security patch, how do we patch without impacting production keys?

[07:54] Lina Chen: connector is typically deployed in customer env so patching follows your change control. we recommend a blue/green deploy for the connector, test with a small canary workload, then cutover. for zero-downtime, have multiple connector instances behind a load balancer. the connector is stateless for crypto; state remains in the HSM and in redwood's metadata store.

[08:22] Carlos Mendez: you said connector is stateless for crypto — is there any cached secret stored on the connector node? like encrypted tokens?

[08:30] Lina Chen: connector stores short-lived tokens and encrypted config; tokens are ephemeral and rotated frequently. nothing long-term. we can also run the connector as a sidecar in a hardened environment for extra control.

[08:44] Jordan Park: i'd like to surface a question that often comes up — certification vs attestation. customers often want a vendor-level FIPS cert. we don't certify hardware on behalf of customers, but we provide the list of FIPS-validated modules and the integration guidance. if you need vendor attestation for the full stack we can walk that process with legal/compliance.

[09:07] Priya Kapoor: that distinction is okay, we mainly need to show the HSMs have FIPS certs and that our deployment meets the controls. can you provide the exact model numbers and cert PDFs?

[09:16] Jordan Park: yes — action item for me to upload the certs and a short mapping doc.

[09:22] Ethan Ross: can we talk about key wrapping algorithm options? we're a safety-critical environment and prefer RSA-OAEP for wrapping but also curious about AES-GCM wrapping.

[09:31] Lina Chen: we support both. HSM will expose wrap/unwrap with your preferred algorithms; for higher throughput we usually use AES-GCM or AES-KW for symmetric wrap and RSA-OAEP for asymmetric. we'll capture recommended ciphers per HSM model in the runbook.

[09:53] Carlos Mendez: audit collectors — you mentioned signed digests earlier. where do you store the signatures and how are they validated?

[09:59] Lina Chen: we sign log blocks with a signing key. for customers who require an external sig, we can push the digest to your KMS or to a transparency log. validation is straightforward: compare the recorded digest with the hash of the logs you retrieved. we'll give a script for that.

[10:20] Priya Kapoor: one more on retention — our legal wants proof of deletion that is irreversible for certain datasets when required. does object lock prevent deletion? how do you handle an auditor requesting proof that a key was destroyed?

[10:31] Lina Chen: for key destruction we support HSM key zeroization which is irreversible by design. we log the zeroize operation with a signed timestamp and provide attestation artifacts. for object lock, you can configure retention windows — after that window an admin can delete with multi-party approval and we log the deletion steps.

[10:58] Jordan Park: ok shifting to a concrete proposal: we'd like to run a 2-hour smoke test in your staging environment. lina will attempt to connect the KMIP/PKCS11 connector to your staging HSM, perform a wrap/unwrap, run a rotation, and push audit logs to your S3 with object lock enabled. proposal is week of Jan 18.

[11:18] Priya Kapoor: that works — we will need a list of pre-reqs for staging, network ports, certs, and what access you'll need.

[11:25] Lina Chen: i'll prepare a staging checklist. quick notes now: port 5696 for KMIP, PKCS11 via an SSH tunnel if on-prem, client cert for mTLS, IAM role for S3 write with restricted permissions, and a small test account in your SCIM directory for RBAC testing.

[11:44] Ethan Ross: echoing that — we'll create a staging VPC and provide a bastion. can you also provide the exact docker image or package version to run the connector? we want to pre-approve hashes with our vulnerability scanning.

[11:56] Lina Chen: absolutely — i'll post the image sha256 and package signature. we also publish SBOM and CVE history for connector releases.

[12:08] Carlos Mendez: what about on-call and incident response? if there's a compromised key, what's the playbook?

[12:15] Jordan Park: we have an incident runbook. short version: rotate compromised key, failover to fallback model if configured (e.g., rotate to a cloud-managed key temporarily), revoke sessions tied to the key, and provide forensic log bundles. for dedicated customers we offer a higher-touch incident response SLA.

[12:36] Priya Kapoor: can you share a redacted incident playbook? auditors like to see the steps.

[12:42] Jordan Park: yes i'll share a redacted playbook in the next 48 hours.

[12:47] Ethan Ross: small question on key policy — can you restrict which services in our account can request unwrap operations? we need least privilege at the service level.

[12:56] Lina Chen: yes, policies are service-principal aware. you can define granular policies that allow only certain service IDs to call unwrap for specific key ids. those policies are enforced at the orchestrator, and we log any policy denials.

[13:16] Priya Kapoor: on the SOC2 docs you mentioned — does the SOC2 scope include your HSM connector or just the control plane?

[13:24] Jordan Park: it covers our control plane and operational controls; the connector is customer-managed. we map the connector responsibilities in the shared responsibility matrix. i'll include that mapping in the artifact upload.

[13:36] Carlos Mendez: a question on billing and costs tied to HSM operations — do you meter per unwrap call if we keep master in our HSM?

[13:44] Jordan Park: usage-based billing still applies for inference tokens and request volume. for cryptographic operations, we bill a lightweight connector usage fee and optional HSM proxy throughput tier. we can give an estimated TCO with a sample workload.

[14:02] Priya Kapoor: that helps for our procurement team. can we get a simple pricing sheet for the staging trial?

[14:08] Jordan Park: yes i'll include a trial pricing appendix.

[14:13] Ethan Ross: one more technical: can we rotate client certs for the connector automatically through a CA? we prefer short-lived certs from our internal PKI rather than static ones.

[14:22] Lina Chen: supported. we can integrate with your internal PKI via ACME or an enterprise CA. connector supports automated cert enrollment with cert rotation hooks.

[14:35] Priya Kapoor: ok i'm going to summarize and then we can close: 1) redwood to share FIPS cert PDFs and HSM model matrix; 2) redwood to share connector image hashes, SBOM, and runbook; 3) redwood to share redacted incident playbook and SOC2 artifacts; 4) meridian to share region/residency matrix and staging access; 5) schedule 2-hour staging test (target week of Jan 18). did i miss anything?

[14:56] Jordan Park: that's perfect. lina anything to add?

[15:01] Lina Chen: i'll also include the sample verification scripts for audit digest validation and tool for verifying log chain integrity. and a sample policy template for service-level RBAC.

[15:12] Carlos Mendez: great. one last comment — we'll loop in procurement for escrow contract language; that might add a week.

[15:19] Jordan Park: understood, thanks. we'll be flexible on timelines.

[15:25] Priya Kapoor: thanks everyone. looking forward to the runbook and the staging checklist.

[15:30] Jordan Park: thanks all — we'll follow up with links within 24-48 hours. meeting adjourned.

[15:40] Post-call notes (auto): Links to upload: SOC2 + ISO package: https://redwood.internal/artifacts/CRM-392174 (access controlled). HSM runbook draft: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/hsm-connector-v1.2. Staging checklist: (will be attached to ticket).

End of transcript.
